A live tier-2 predicate handed an input it cannot measure refuses per this section's measurement rule, whatever the tier's face: the input is the actor's own, the repair is theirs, and the tier's escape stands open beneath the refusal. **Unmeasurable** covers both shapes: a degraded measurement environment, and an out-of-domain input — a subject whose bytes are not valid in the measuring charmap has no codepoint count, and a naive length that returns a confident decimal over such bytes is not a measurement. The refusal's cause and audit record are content-free: the arm name and the measured decimal where one exists, never the subject bytes (§3.8's refusal-record rule; §3.11's hostile-arm terseness).

**One inventory, one home.** The inventory lives at `.pi/extensions/ghjig/postures.ts` and covers every dependency the enforcement layer stands on — all three tiers, not only the runtime that hosts the file. Posture rows are declarative data carrying their justification in place, read by reviewers and checks, never resolved at decision time by the components they describe: a tier whose postures are compiled into its own control flow (the local tier's fail-open chain, §3.2) is inventoried there with no runtime reader owed, so one home serves the layer without a cross-runtime dependency. A posture declared in a shipped enforcement source outside that file is a second home for the property — §3.11's divergence surface, not redundancy — and the home binds under §6.1's inventory rule through a structural check that fails on exactly that shape.

Dependency-load failure is observable **uniformly**: every load site emits the same typed warning through the same channel, because one site warning while a sibling site fails silently hides the second consumer — the exact shape a uniform rule exists to prevent. A site that structurally cannot warn (the bootstrap that loads the warning machinery itself) is named as the exception rather than left implicit. And when a load fails because a caller passed a wrong path, the fix lands at the **call site**, never in a loader taught to guess: a guessing loader silently rescues genuinely wrong paths and erodes its own signal until a warning no longer implies its condition.

Measurement is a **total function with exactly two outcomes** — a valid value, or nothing plus a failure — and no consumer ever reads an unvalidated value. An unmeasurable predicate refuses; it never approves: an out-of-domain value that errors both sides of a comparison must not collapse the check to "valid". A degraded measurement environment refuses **only the inputs it would mis-measure**; inputs it still measures exactly keep passing, so degradation never blocks wider than the actual loss. Where a measurement failure radiates into callers that consume it for other purposes, that blast radius is disclosed at the contract, not discovered in operation. And a gate that cannot determine what an action will actually land on requires the actor to make the target explicit rather than guessing it from a proxy — an unverifiable destination is ambiguity, and ambiguity fails toward the block.

The norm is **procedural today**, enforced at review (§2.3); the posture inventory is homed above, and its remaining instruments derive per §1.2's macro-phase clause.

### 3.10 Delegated computation

A component that delegates work to an external interpreter or tool under a fail-closed contract admits the result on **output validity alone** — never on the process's exit status, and never on a presence probe. Both answer a question the contract does not ask ("did something run?") in place of the one it does ("may I use this result?"). The fail-closed set is enumerated **by outcome, not by cause**: the delegate absent; a failed run; a run that succeeded with junk output; a run that succeeded partially; and the payload landing on the wrong stream. A status-only test decides exactly two of those five and silently accepts the rest.

What failing closed *means* depends on the component's role. A **pre-processor** that cannot vouch for its output returns the input **unchanged**, so the gate still runs against the full text — an unreduced input can only over-match, a recoverable false block, while admitted junk under-matches, a silent wrong allow. A consumer that **iterates** a result set treats empty-but-well-formed as suspect — a completed check that checked nothing is indistinguishable at the call site from all-clear — so its validity predicate is *valid AND non-empty*. And where **every** byte string is a legitimate output, no predicate over the output alone can work; validity is established by a framing protocol a degraded producer cannot satisfy, never inspected as a shape. A lossy fallback **refuses** what it cannot process rather than answering a different, weaker question: a weaker parse is a second implementation reaching its own verdicts silently. And a tool that rewrites a tracked file is **transactional**: it validates before mutating, builds the result out of place, replaces atomically, and no-ops when already converged — a torn or partial write is a silent wrong allow against every reader of that file.

**Freshness is validated on both operands.** A time-to-live comparison against an unvalidated clock reading is not a bound at all, and the validation precedes the arithmetic its own failure could skip — an error that unwinds past the decision point leaves zero records, the worst failure shape, detectable only by counting records against a known-good control. Failure classes are keyed by **outcome shape, not mechanism**: one intuitive label ("non-numeric") can span several mechanisms with different verdicts, so the guard rejects on shape rather than patching any one mechanism. A guarded surface must not host inputs that can disarm its own guard — a write the guard itself permits must not be able to forge the guard's decisions — and the mitigation for such a class applies **uniformly, with an empty exemption set and a structural lock**, so a new site cannot drift in unguarded.

The norm is **procedural today**, enforced at review (§2.3); instruments derive with the gates that delegate to them per §1.2's macro-phase clause.

### 3.11 Gate design

**Enforcement physics.** An irreversible-class norm may not rest on a bypassable tier alone — it needs an unbypassable backstop (§3.2's tier 3), with the local check as that same rule's fast-feedback **pre-image**: one predicate, two call sites. The local check runs the very rule the remote gate runs, so "clean locally" and "clean at the gate" cannot diverge by construction. For the gate classes that predate this section, the backstop obligation is satisfied amortized: each named irreversible class gains its unbypassable home through its own §3.3 derivation cycle, and until then the gap stands as a declared deferral, not an oversight. Where no unbypassable layer ever sees the guarded act, there is no such home to gain, and the class's row records that residual in place (§3.3).

**Ownership and affordances.** Each gate class has exactly one owning enforcement point — ownership binds to the **predicate**: other tiers are call sites of that one rule (or, where a platform-native site cannot literally share code, implementations converged against the recorded shape §4.3 keeps), never second implementations — a second home for the same property is a divergence surface, not redundancy. A remedy's guard mirrors its gate's predicate exactly: a remedy looser than the gate it repairs deadlocks the flow at the gap between them. An evidence producer's predicate is at least as strict as its consumer's, single-sourced — where the two must differ, the producer fails on the retractable side, never the published side. Every enforced gate owes an **in-flow authoring affordance** that repairs rather than reports — a gate with no authoring-side affordance manufactures post-hoc repair commits — and the affordance references the gate's rule source, never re-derives it. A report-only check names the property it does **not** establish, so a green report is never read as the missing guarantee. Gates bind at the irreversible moment, not the authoring moment; an annotation that adds no claim carries no gate; and a ruling that narrows nothing needs no new gate.

**Remediation is arm-scoped** — the sharpened form of §3.5's positive-remediation rule. Every arm reachable by a plausible honest mistake names its own **live** recovery: where a shared checker serves several enforcement surfaces, the checker emits the cause and each calling surface appends the recovery that is actually live there, because one recovery string baked into the shared checker is dead at the other surfaces — a message naming a dead recovery is worse than one naming none. Arms reachable only by hostile input stay deliberately terse: there is no honest recovery to name, and drafting one coaches the attempt. An arm whose entire output is a status code delegates the positive face to its caller — the obligation binds wherever a message surface exists, and never requires growing one. Two failure shapes get two distinct block messages: "the evidence is missing" (remedy: produce it) and "the lookup failed" (remedy: re-run).

**Semantics essentials**, binding every gate class that touches them:

- Protection binds to what a ref **is**, never to its literal name; a differently-cased or aliased spelling of the same ref is the same ref.
- History-rewrite gates key on whether the history is **shared**, never on the command's name; a local rewrite is free, a published one is gated.
- The merged state must **be** the reviewed state: unverified local work waiting behind a verified head blocks the merge.
- Authority fields — identity, subject binding, freshness — are read from the platform-attested object; only the verdict itself is read from authored text.
- Approval evidence carries a freshness predicate: it must postdate its subject's last change, and an out-of-window pass over-blocks, never silently allows.
- Removing the classification that selects an artifact's governance regime is itself a gated act, whoever performs it.
- A platform's auto-close keyword channel is a gate surface: an evidence-gated artifact must not be closable by a trailer in some other artifact's body.
- Allow decisions are non-terminal and any block terminates, so gate composition is order-independent — no ordering can convert a block into an allow.
- A gate enumerates, in place, the bypass vectors it deliberately does not model, so a residual reads as a decision rather than an oversight.

The norm is **procedural today**, enforced at review (§2.3); the semantics land per gate class through each class's own Doc → Test → Code derivation cycle (§1.2, §3.3).

### 3.12 Gate verification

A green suite does not prove a guard is live: a silently weakened guard can keep passing assertions that no longer exercise it. Guards are therefore verified by **mutating the guarded artifact** — weaken the rule in a throwaway, isolated copy of the tree, run the suite there, and require it to **fail**; a surviving mutant means no assertion pins that guard, a harness defect, never a tolerated gap. Mutation coverage is prioritized by the same wrong-allow cost asymmetry that selects enforcement faces (§3.6): the gates whose wrong allow is irreversible are the ones whose kill is proven first. This generalizes §1.2's failing-first rule from one test to the guard corpus.

A newly landed gate **cannot be observed by its own landing change** where the platform withholds a gate's execution from the change that introduces it: the landing verifies structure only, and the next change is the gate's first empirical firing. This is a named deferral of §5.3's smallest-change activation probe, not an exemption from it — the probe obligation transfers to the first post-landing change.

**Gate checks must not lie in either direction.** A check that can false-red is a defect: a red that is not a defect destroys the signal readers act on — so a deterministic proxy is preferred over a nondeterministic hard gate, a flaky external fetch is retried and buffered rather than allowed to fail the run, and one leg's failure never masks a sibling's result. The toolchain a gate executes is pinned and integrity-verified fail-closed, re-checked on **every** reuse, and cached where no co-tenant can pre-seed it — a gate that runs an unverified tool is itself an unreviewed write path into the verdict. Gate cost is staged by proximity to irreversibility: fast checks ride every commit; the expensive suite runs at the ready/merge boundary, where the irreversible act it guards actually happens.

The norm is **procedural today**, enforced at review (§2.3); the mutation harness and CI instruments derive later per §1.2's macro-phase clause.

## 4. Substrate and install contract

This section states how shell assets install into a repository: target-parameterized, homed in shell-owned namespaces that collide with no other tooling's, landed through PR-based installs — and kept observably fresh after landing (§4.5). It also states how enforcement binds to and resolves its own inputs (§4.6), and the host boundary installation never crosses (§4.7).

### 4.1 Namespaces

The shell owns exactly two working-tree namespaces in a governed repository: `.pi/` (substrate-native runtime assets — extensions, when tier 1 lands) and `.ghjig/` (per-clone untracked state — the shell binding, never committed). Repository-visible substrate lives in standard platform locations: `.github/` (templates, workflows), `.githooks/` (the local tier), `changelog_unreleased/` (the fragment tree). The shell installs nothing into a namespace owned by other tooling, and enforced behavior never depends on such a namespace existing.

The local tier's delegated helpers (§3.2) are committed at `.githooks/helpers/` — a subdirectory of the standard location above, so the placement mints no third shell-owned namespace. The subdirectory is inert to the layer that hosts it: git executes only the top-level hook-named files of a configured hooks path, so nothing under `helpers/` runs except through an adapter's delegation. Committing the helpers adds no resolution path: an adapter reaches a helper directory only through the per-clone untracked binding (§3.2), which a clone may point anywhere — `.githooks/helpers/` is where the bytes live, not how they are found — and those bytes are clone-independent per §4.2, with anything clone-specific still generated under `.ghjig/`.

### 4.2 Target-parameterization

Committed substrate carries no absolute paths, no clone-specific values, and no knowledge of any particular development environment's layout. Anything clone-specific — above all the binding to whatever runtime backs the local tier — is generated per-clone as untracked state under `.ghjig/` (§3.2). The same committed bytes must work in every clone of every adopting repository.

### 4.3 PR-based installs

Substrate lands in an adopting repository through the standard flow — a reviewed PR (§1.1) — never a direct push. The one exception is the stage-0 seed of an empty repository (an unborn default branch cannot host a PR); that seed is minimal (the direction documents), scoped, and audit-logged. Server-side configuration (labels, the branch ruleset, board mirrors) is applied via the platform API; the repository records the shape server config must match — above all that required-check contexts equal the CI job names (`fragment-gate`, `ssot-home`, `toc-freshness`) and that the default branch's allowed merge method is the merge commit alone (§1.1).

### 4.4 Headless and scripted operation

Any scripted install, verify, or test step that drives the substrate honors the constraints recorded in the issue #4 spike note: headless invocations receive an explicit end-of-input on stdin and pass the explicit project-trust flag, and scripted-provider configurations supply the required placeholder endpoint value. Install tooling that ignores these hangs or fails spuriously; the spike note is the pinned reference for the observed behaviors.

### 4.5 Installed-asset freshness

An asset materialized into a target at install time — copied or linked files, as opposed to behavior resolved live through a binding — drifts silently when the shell later gains or renames assets: the target keeps working with yesterday's set, and no error names the cause. The shell owes drift **detection**, not auto-repair: a session-start advisory compares the shipped asset set against the installed set and, on a gap, names the missing assets and the exact re-sync command — never mutating the target uninvited — **report-don't-mutate**, the same posture as §4.3's PR-based installs, which land change only through the reviewed flow.

Remedy text distinguishes the two gap shapes: one a session restart fixes (the shell itself gained the asset mid-session, so the running session is behind its own tree) and one only a re-install fixes (the target's installed set predates the asset). The re-sync remedy is an install re-run — idempotent by §4.7's contract, so prescribing it is always safe. A wrong prescribed remedy at the failure site is itself a defect this section exists to prevent. The norm is **explicitly advisory** (§3.1 rule 1): a freshness advisory, never a block.

### 4.6 Binding and resolution

**Ambient never on the hot path.** The ambient environment is never an input on the enforcement hot path: every enforcement entry point self-locates from its own installed location, so a stale global setting cannot redirect which rule tree loads — the cross-clone contamination vector, where one clone's stale export makes another clone's enforcement load the wrong rules. A running session's hot path must not depend on a name the change under way is renaming — otherwise the rename disarms the very session performing it. Exactly one documented override seam exists, marked test-only, and an active seam announces itself in a live session (§5.9); a retired input is cut cleanly — never honored, never shimmed — with a live signal that it is now ignored.

**Write-target equals read-target.** The path an evidence or registration producer writes must be exactly the path the consuming gate reads: a divergence silently fails the gate open with no error anywhere — the write succeeds, the read finds nothing, and both report clean. Audit destinations resolve to a real, durable location in every execution context except the test-run class §5.5 carves out, where teardown loss is the intent; anywhere else, a destination keyed to a disposable working copy loses the record at teardown. Relocated state keeps a read-only legacy floor: writers move unconditionally to the new location, and readers consult the old one only when the new one is absent, never in preference to it — §2.5(c)'s install-boundary premise, applied to state.

**Registry-scoped, fail-open, physically matched.** Enforcement is scoped by a registry of governed paths and is transparently inert outside it — a guardrail, not a sandbox: every scope-guard failure mode fails open, so a broken guard can only under-enforce, never lock the operator out of unrelated work (§5.2's aid direction; the evidence gates inside the scope keep their own fail-closed contracts). Scope matching compares resolved physical paths with boundary normalization, so a symlinked working directory or a path-prefix collision cannot mis-scope enforcement in either direction. And a detector cannot live inside the path whose failure it detects — a broken-binding check reached through that binding never runs in exactly the failure it exists to catch — so that detection relocates to the launch path that runs before the binding is traversed.

The norm is **procedural today**, enforced at review (§2.3); binding instruments derive with the runtime a clone binds to per §1.2's macro-phase clause.

### 4.7 Host boundary

Installation and operation leave the host untouched outside governed repositories: no home-directory configuration, no shell login files, no global version-control settings, no path registration, no background services or auto-start hooks. Disabling the shell is ceasing to invoke it; no uninstall procedure exists, because nothing global was installed. An installer's allowed actions are enumerated — dependency checks and creating its own directories — and package-manager invocations and privilege escalation sit outside them. Governed repositories are the one named carve-out where mutation is intended (§4.3), and even there an install never overwrites a pre-existing same-named asset: it skips, warns, and names the remedy — the target's choice wins. Install and registration are idempotent and re-runnable: the re-sync remedy §4.5 prescribes must exist and be safe to repeat. Shell-created untracked files inside a governed repository are excluded from that repository's version control at creation, not by convention (§4.1's untracked-state contract; §5.5 governs the ungoverned-repository case).

A repository binds at its root only, never recursively into subprojects: a nested or unadopted project inside the working scope keeps its own configuration untouched. Platform queries are pinned to the repository under work — an unpinned lookup silently answers about a different repository or host — and an unresolvable pin fails closed.

The norm is **procedural today**, enforced at review (§2.3); install instruments derive later per §1.2's macro-phase clause.

## 5. Cross-cutting contracts

This section states the contracts that bind every section: self-contained artifacts, graceful degradation for best-effort automations, explicit activation conditions for gates that sleep until their subject exists, the state boundary shell-written state honors (§5.5), the operating modes that set the autonomy ceiling (§5.6), the conduct an unattended run owes (§5.7), the context lifecycle (§5.8), and the session surfaces (§5.9).

### 5.1 Self-contained artifacts

Every durable artifact in a governed repository — this SPEC included — states its rationale from first principles and cites only artifacts that resolve in-repo: files, issues, PRs, and commits of this repository. No external project, foreign specification, or agent-specific tooling is normative, and "another project does it this way" is never a rationale. The one legitimate external subject is the pi substrate itself, grounded through `MISSION.md`. Names of specific agents, models, or vendors do not appear in committed bytes; interfaces owned by an external runtime are confined to per-clone untracked state (§4.2). A mechanical token sweep as a CI gate class is a candidate refinement; until it exists, the norm is enforced at review (§2.3, §2.4).

### 5.2 Graceful degradation

A best-effort automation fails **open with a surfaced signal**, never closed and never silently: a missing optional dependency, an incomplete helper, or an unreachable service degrades the automation to a no-op or a warning — it does not wedge git, block the flow, or misattribute a cause. The recorded shape: the local tier's advisory-face guard (§3.2) turns a present-but-incomplete helper into a no-op instead of a false block. Degradation of an **enforcing** gate is different: a gate that fails must fail *closed* on its own evidence check (a missing pass comment blocks the flip; an unresolvable review blocks the merge) — fail-open is for best-effort aids, fail-closed for evidence gates, and every gate's contract says which it is. A silently degraded state is surfaced at the next session start where a session surface exists — the advisory names the degraded capability and the exact re-arm command (§4.5 is the asset-set instance; the surface's own conduct is §5.9); until such a surface exists for a given tier, the silence is recorded here as a known gap (the known instance: an unregistered clone's local tier no-ops with no notice), and the fail-open direction itself stays definitional.

### 5.3 Gate-activation conditions

A gate whose subject does not yet exist **sleeps clean and says so**: its skip condition is part of its contract, stated where the gate is implemented (observed: `check-toc.yml` and `check-ssot-home.sh` skip while no `SPEC.md` exists, and each names that condition in its own text). Two obligations follow: the skip must be a deliberate branch, not an accidental fall-through; and a sleeping gate's **first activation is probed at the smallest possible change** — the change that creates the subject is pushed and verified against the real CI environment before anything larger rides on the gate (this SPEC's own PR exercised exactly that probe — issue #5). The one named deferral of the probe — a gate whose execution the platform withholds from its own landing change — lives at §3.12.

### 5.4 Work language

Durable artifacts are authored in the repository's configured work language (default: English); the conversational language of any particular working session is a separate channel and never leaks into committed artifacts. One artifact, one language — mixed-language durable artifacts are a defect.

### 5.5 State boundary

The shell governs work in repositories that adopt it (§0.1), and its write scope ends where that governance ends, the same way its install scope ends at its own namespaces (§4.1). Per-project shell state — audit records, caches, working files — is therefore written only inside governed repositories. A state write whose working directory falls in a repository the shell does **not** govern must either fall through to shell-owned storage or exclude the created path from that repository's version control at creation — shell state carries operational text — an audit record names locators, categories, and command *shapes*, with any free text encoded at write time so one record stays one line, and it never carries the content a refusal withheld (§3.8): a secret match reports its pattern identity, never the matched text (§3.6) — and even that reduced text must never become committable history in a repository the shell does not control. The same reasoning binds the record at rest: a state file the shell creates is readable only by the account that writes it, because an audit record names what a repository's work touched and a host may carry accounts that work never concerned. Its plausible false-block cost is nil — the mode governs who may read a file the shell alone writes, so no legitimate flow is refused (§3.6 obligation (i)). The boundary has a second face inside governed repositories: an execution context that exists to exercise the shell — a test or verification run — resolves shell state to a disposable root and never writes the operational sinks the calibration loop reads (§3.6); a suite that pollutes the evidence surface corrupts every decision read from it.

The residual is two-sided: exclusion-at-creation mutates a foreign repository's local metadata (a cost), fall-through loses per-repo locality (a cost). The implementing issue decides between them; either way, the unexcluded-committable outcome is the defect. The norm is **procedural today**, enforced at review (§2.3); the write-path instrument derives later per §1.2's macro-phase clause.

### 5.6 Operating modes

Autonomy is an explicit, resolvable setting, never an inference from context. **Attended** — the default — stops at the ready transition (§2.3), the last decision before the irreversible boundary, and hands the decision to a human. **Unattended** — an opt-in — continues through merge-or-park (§5.7) and no further. Public, unretractable acts — a version tag, a public release, publication into a repository the shell does not govern — sit past the ceiling in every mode.

Resolution is layered — an invocation-scoped override, then the environment, then per-project state, then the default — and an unknown value fails safe, naming the offending source. **Fail-safe has no universal direction**: the safe fallback is set by what the toggle guards — an autonomy toggle falls back toward more human, an integrity toggle toward more gate, an unconfirmable publish toward silence. Per-project configuration never lives on a surface shared across projects (§5.5's boundary, applied to configuration).

Mode changes **who consumes a verdict, never whether a gate runs**: automation never suppresses a review gate. Every checkpoint that expects a human confirmation declares its designated fallback decider, so the flow is operationally complete with no human present — a reviewer verdict may substitute for the human slot at judgment checkpoints (plan approval, the ready decision), but identity-attributed evidence acts (§2.2's trusted-account activation verdict) stay account-bound in every mode. Substitution reaches judgment, never attribution.

The norm is **explicitly advisory** today (§3.1 rule 1), enforced at review (§2.3); the mode instruments derive later per §1.2's macro-phase clause.

### 5.7 Unattended conduct

An unattended run classifies what stopped it before acting: **clean** — nothing blocks; **soft** — attributable to the run's own last change and fixable without a new product decision; **hard** — needing a decision only a human can make. A clean state proceeds to the ceiling action (§5.6). A soft blocker earns exactly one self-repair attempt; a second soft outcome escalates to hard — a second rejection demands another materially different method (§1.4's round-2 mandate), which is itself the new product decision that makes the blocker hard. A hard blocker **parks**: a deterministic state summary, a marker label, a log entry, and an audit record — idempotent on repeat, and itself a friction signal the calibration loop (§3.6) reads. Parking is the named next action, never a bare stop.

**Generation is open, decision is gated.** The shell may produce any artifact unattended — drafts, proposals, candidate corrections — but every state transition stays behind its gate: completing a scoping-tier item, applying an SSOT correction, or discarding another party's filed work is never a side effect of an unattended run. An unattended sweep never reverses a deliberate human act — a human-set blocked state is not auto-cleared. It never re-adjudicates an unchanged artifact — batch idempotence keys on subject freshness, so a verdict postdating the subject's last edit stands. And it never destroys an untrusted filer's content — a rejected outside filing is demoted to the friction-free tier (§2.1) with a lineage link, and a trusted filer's item is never auto-closed.

**No actor satisfies a gate on its own behalf.** Where an own-artifact approval is admissible at all, it is a per-project, default-off, operator-set policy — and even then the evidence rules of §1.6 bind it in full.

The norm is **explicitly advisory** today (§3.1 rule 1), enforced at review (§2.3); the classifier and park instruments derive later per §1.2's macro-phase clause.

### 5.8 Context lifecycle

Working context is a managed resource, and the destructive reset is the last resort — narrowing what enters context (§1.5's bounded distillations, §2.8's budgeted surfaces) comes first. **A context discard is archive-then-discard, never delete**: before any discard, task-scoped state is distilled into at least one durable artifact, its field set defined by what a restore needs — the branch, the issue, the change under way, the phase, the next step. Reconstruction then reuses the one existing injection path rather than minting a parallel surface that can drift from it. Where the shell cannot intercept an outer discard mechanism, it front-loads the invariant: the archive step precedes the discard, and the trigger stays explicit — a wrong discard is irreversible within a session, exactly the cost shape that forbids automating it (§3.6).

Retrieval over durable memory is structurally bounded: a recall surface returns pointers whose worst-case cost is fixed and stated, never bodies — following a pointer is a separate, targeted read. The expensive deep tier is reachable only by explicit intent, with one bounded escalation permitted when the cheap tier misses on a substantive ask: the cheap miss already realized is the signal that justifies the spend. Cost-of-miss asymmetry governs affordances the way it governs faces (§3.6): a cheap recoverable miss earns an automatic nudge; an expensive one earns explicit-intent-only. Recurring advisories are rate-limited by design — an every-turn signal trains its reader to ignore it — and state read back from durable storage is validated at the boundary, never trusted as written (§3.9).

The norm is **explicitly advisory** (§3.1 rule 1): context economy is never a gate; the lifecycle instruments derive later per §1.2's macro-phase clause.

### 5.9 Session surfaces

Session-start work is time-boxed and staleness-stamped: an expensive check runs behind a time-to-live stamp, is wrapped in a timeout so a hung dependency never stalls startup, degrades to silence on error (§5.2's aid direction), and stamps only after a successful compute — a failed run must not debounce the next attempt. The recurring surface is one debounced, actionable line per degraded state, naming the state and its exact re-arm command (§5.2), kept alongside any per-invocation diagnostic floor — the once-per-session line is for the operator, the per-invocation line for the log reader, and neither replaces the other. A new measuring signal ships stating its own false-positive shapes and runs on demand until its precision is observed; only then does it earn an always-on surface — §3.6's measure step, applied to the measuring device itself. Check cadence derives from compute cost: a cheap presence check runs every session, while an expensive or privileged one stays occasional with its deferral named.

The disarm bar binds every surface: no enforcement-disabling state may be both reachable by one innocuous command and traceless — making a disarmed state observable is a separate, cheaper decision than changing its fail direction, so observability never waits on a posture debate. And a detector mirrors the resolution order of the consumer it protects — reading the fallback exactly where the consumer would — or it is blind exactly where the consumer is live (§4.6's detector-placement rule is the structural limit case).

The norm is **explicitly advisory** (§3.1 rule 1); the surfaces derive later per §1.2's macro-phase clause.

## 6. Self-governance milestone

This section states the criterion for the point at which this repository's own development runs under the shell it ships, and the standing posture each shell mechanism holds toward the substrate beneath it (§6.1).

The milestone is reached when both hold:

1. **Tier 1 self-applied** — the in-process gate for a class §3.3 homes at tier 1 loads from this repository's own tree in the sessions that develop this repository, blocking the norm violations it specifies here.
2. **Tier 2 self-bound** — the per-clone adapter (§3.2) in this repository's development clones binds to the runtime this repository ships, not to any external one.

Until then, an external development environment may govern the working process, under one absolute condition: it never surfaces in committed artifacts (§5.1). After the milestone, this repository is its own first adopter, and every norm in this SPEC is exercised on the shell's own development before any adopter meets it.

### 6.1 Substrate posture

The substrate under the shell is a rising floor: it improves under use and absorbs generic agent-support machinery over time. A shell mechanism that merely re-does what the substrate now does natively is redundant cost; the shell's durable value concentrates where a general substrate structurally cannot go — opinionated engineering policy, high-asymmetry safety redundancy (§3.6), and repository artifacts as durable memory. Each shell mechanism therefore carries exactly one standing posture — **cede to the substrate**, **keep as policy**, or **keep as safety redundancy** — and a cede is a forward-discipline signal retired through its own change on the standard flow (§1.1), never an in-place deletion. §3.1 caps the classification: an enforcement-layer mechanism never resolves to cede on the strength of substrate-grown permissions — its floor posture is keep-as-safety-redundancy, because the only-safety-net commitment is substrate-evolution-proof by definition.

Where this SPEC claims to classify a family exhaustively, a parity check fails until every member has its row; and an inventory this SPEC states is machine-checked against the real tree, or it rots — §2.4's clause that an exact count belongs where going stale fails a check, applied to trees. This SPEC also owes its own falsifiable acceptance checklist — observable, all-must-hold conditions read before the shell operates on a repository — committed to here and derived later like this section's parity and inventory checks. And build order follows consumption order — shared contracts before their consumers, templates before their readers, one end-to-end path proven before self-application (this section's milestone).

The norm is **explicitly advisory** (§3.1 rule 1): a design doctrine; the parity and inventory checks and the acceptance checklist derive later per §1.2's macro-phase clause.
